questions.q: What does the `--zones 1 2 3` flag do when creating the AKS cluster and its node pools?
options: It limits the cluster to exactly 3 nodes forever
It spreads the node pool's VMs across all three availability zones in the region, so losing one zone doesn't take down the whole cluster
It sets the cluster's time zone for logging
It creates 3 separate clusters, one per zone
questions.explain: Availability zones are physically separate datacenter facilities with independent power and networking; spreading nodes across all three is what gives the cluster zone-level fault tolerance.

questions.q: Why does Theo create a separate `apppool` node pool in `User` mode instead of running everything on the default pool?
options: User mode pools are cheaper
It keeps Kubernetes's own system workloads from competing for capacity with checkout-api, catalog-api, and cart-api during a traffic spike
System pools can't run application workloads at all
AKS requires at least two pools by law
questions.explain: Separating a dedicated User mode pool for the storefront services from the System pool is a real best practice that avoids resource contention.

questions.q: What does the checkout-api HorizontalPodAutoscaler in this lesson do?
options: Nothing — it's just a label
Scales checkout-api's replica count between 6 and 30 based on CPU utilization averaging 65%
Automatically rewrites the Deployment's image tag
Moves pods between availability zones
questions.explain: The HPA targets the checkout-api Deployment and scales replicas from a minimum of 6 to a maximum of 30 based on CPU utilization crossing 65%.

questions.q: What is specifically absent from the checkout-api Deployment manifest in this lesson, and why does it matter?
options: Resource requests and limits — the Deployment has none
topologySpreadConstraints or podAntiAffinity — without either, the scheduler can freely concentrate pods onto nodes in the same availability zone
A container image reference
A namespace
questions.explain: The manifest has resource requests/limits, a readiness probe, and an HPA, but nothing telling the scheduler how to spread checkout-api's pods across zones or nodes.

questions.q: Why doesn't this gap show up as a problem while Theo is validating the cluster in this lesson?
options: Because the gap doesn't actually exist

Because at low replica counts on a freshly built, evenly empty node pool, pod placement tends to look even regardless — the gap only matters under a fast scale-out driven by genuinely uneven real traffic
Because AKS automatically fixes uneven placement after one hour
Because checkout-api doesn't use the HPA yet
questions.explain: The gap is real but quiet: it takes a specific kind of event — a rapid scale-out under real, uneven sale traffic — for uneven AZ placement to actually become visible, which is exactly what Lessons 8 and 9 build toward.
